blocks.x: Live-service backend on capacity discipline, session infrastructure cost down 31% and launch-day concurrency 3.4x served without incident

A gaming company: Product companies feel platform gaps in churn and support cost, both visible in cohort data. The Achala program started with the release pipeline —. The baseline signed in week two made the cost visible in units the finance team already owns, and the engagement ran under the standard Achala charter — a named metric, a named control owner and gates that evidence every move.

The baseline launch post-mortem priced the improvisation: concurrency beyond 40% of forecast caused queue cascades, infrastructure spend doubled for a week and settled too late, and one matchmaking outage trended before the game did.
Capacity planning used peak-of-peak folklore; the real session shape, joins, matches, store traffic, lived unmeasured in fleets of similar-but-not-identical services.

We gave the live service a capacity spine: session-shape telemetry decomposed per service, load models built from real shapes, game-day rehearsals at 150% of forecast concurrency, adaptive scaling policies per service class with the cost ledger visible, and the launch readiness gate requiring a passed rehearsal. The next launch trended for the right reasons.
